Systems in context

From the control-room console to a railway observation

Inspect the physical equipment, then separate the source, delivery, presentation and record of information.

Start with what occupies the room

A control centre contains workstations, display surfaces, communications terminals, cable routes and the technical equipment serving them. These are useful physical subjects for an anatomy model. A desk is not a responsibility, and a hardware cabinet is not the software function it hosts. The room in this atlas is an original composition with empty consoles and fixed furniture. Open a console or cabinet to inspect its construction. People, task allocation, incident coordination and duty handover belong to the separate People & processes pages. This separation lets the equipment view answer where things are and how they connect without pretending to reproduce an operator’s facility.

IRSE Netherlands · Health and Safety Executive

Separate the monitor from its information

The console view contains a display panel, controller and supply boards, enclosure, keyboard, pointing device, communications handset and computer interface. A local computer can sit near its peripherals. A remote arrangement can place computing equipment elsewhere and connect it through an interface that carries display and input information. Public KVM products illustrate this distinction; they are one possible technology family. The atlas’s alternatives change the physical hardware and add a shared presentation surface. They do not establish a universal network architecture or transfer operating responsibility. Play the example and watch the picture change only when the delivery stage reaches it.

G&D / Panoptec Europe · Barco · Health and Safety Executive

Locate the host, network, gateway and recorder

The technical-room cabinets expose main boards, storage carriers, switching interfaces, patching and a UPS battery cassette. Their functions differ. A network carries information between endpoints; an application organizes it; a gateway meets a different system’s interface; a recorder stores information; a presentation controller supplies a display. Software functions may share hardware or be distributed. The cabinet counts and module arrangement here are teaching choices. The UPS provides a separate power dependency, without assigning a runtime or proving that an application survives every interruption. There is no freestanding physical table for an event timeline: history appears on a monitor, and its storage hardware is separately selectable.

Siemens Mobility · ABB · Moxa · Barco

Follow a request and a separately returned observation

Information behaviour uses a two-dimensional topology because locations, direction and state matter more than the shape of a rack. A selected request passes from the console through network, application and gateway boundaries to the field interface. Receipt does not establish acceptance or physical completion. A separately reported observation then returns: an occupied section in Traffic, an open breaker indication in Power, or a running-fan indication in Station. The display retains its previous placeholder until delivery reaches it. The final stage appends a source-associated record. This trace does not move points, switch electrical energy or select a station emergency mode. It explains what each receiving endpoint knows at that stage.

Siemens Mobility · Siemens Mobility · Siemens Mobility

Compare the function that is available

Display unavailable removes the task picture while the host and recorder still receive information. This demonstrates a presentation dependency; it does not tell the reader whether remote equipment has failed. Alternate host selects a different application host before playback and delivers information using that selected configuration. It is a comparison, not an automatic failover simulation. No recovery time, synchronized state or continued control authority is assumed. HSE’s control-room guidance supports making relationships between controls, displays and feedback understandable. Apply that question here: what originated the information, which endpoint has received it, and which presentation or record is actually available?

Health and Safety Executive · Siemens Mobility · IRSE Netherlands

Continue into the human work

Equipment and information behaviour provide context for the separate process studies. Acknowledgement, coordination and resolution are different states; a stored record alone does not establish a repaired condition. Duty handover involves relevant information and two-way checking, not a change in furniture. Use the source cards to distinguish an operator or authority example from a supplier product, a public conference abstract or general industrial guidance. None supplies a universal control-room layout or a railway operating procedure.

What happens during a maintenance visit?

Follow the relationship between vehicle condition, yard allocation, technical work, test evidence and the handover back to operations.

A visit begins with a reason for work

A depot combines railway routes with places to inspect, service, repair and test vehicles. A visit may respond to a scheduled interval, a reported fault or condition evidence collected in service. Those starting points do not necessarily require the same road, equipment or duration. Public maintenance facilities combine light servicing with selected overhaul capabilities; other work may go to a specialist component workshop. The useful question is what needs to be established or restored, and what resources the task requires. The depot overview shows the physical destinations; the activity views explain the work that connects them.

Location and readiness are different information

Yard coordination needs to know which vehicle is present, where it is, what destination is available and what work has been assigned. A train can occupy a stabling road while awaiting attention, or be on a maintenance road with work in progress. A location marker therefore says little about readiness by itself. Public yard-management systems bring together occupancy, work status and communication between the people involved. In the yard comparison, changing the destination also changes the point arrangement, vehicle position and work boundary. The highlighted connections explain coordination; they do not prove a route or grant movement authority.

Inspection produces evidence; diagnosis interprets it

A roll-by measurement system observes selected features as a vehicle passes fixed sensors. The measurements may concern wheel profiles, brakes or other visible equipment. Stationary examination can add close inspection, a physical gauge and diagnostic information from the vehicle. These are complementary kinds of evidence. A symptom may belong to a sensor, wiring, controller, actuator or the mechanical equipment itself, so an indication does not automatically identify a replacement part. Compare the two assessment arrangements: one moves the train through a measuring position; the other holds it still beside tools and a diagnostic connection. The model produces no actual defect or acceptance decision.

Running-gear work changes both access and support

An inspection pit provides access beneath a vehicle without removing its running gear. Vehicle lifting and a bogie drop change the support arrangement in different ways; compare the body, attached bogies and fixed supports before following their motion. Once removed, a wheelset can be measured, reprofiled or examined for material condition using an appropriate inspection method. Dimensional measurement and non-destructive inspection answer different questions. The wheelset study adds a probe fixture and a recorded-information connection, while the brake bench shows a caliper applying to a stationary disc. Neither animation supplies a machining limit, inspection technique or brake test instruction.

Doors, climate equipment and traction need their own work

Maintenance extends beyond the wheels and bogies. A door has moving leaves, a drive, guides and observations of its position; on-train servicing and off-train repair address different work scopes. HVAC combines air circulation, heat exchange, refrigeration equipment and controls, with functional testing after relevant work. Traction work can involve electrical machines, bearings and windings, or converter modules and control electronics. The component view uses a converter bench so the equipment study does not depend on which propulsion arrangement is selected elsewhere. Opening covers and separating modules exposes the equipment relationships, while the phase control explains motion or information flow.

A completed repair needs the appropriate evidence

A component test fixture, a stationary vehicle check and a test road offer different ways to observe a function. The required checks follow the task and the applicable instructions; the atlas does not make every vehicle visit follow one sequence. A recorded response must be assessed in its proper context, including the equipment identity and the work performed. Commissioning or accepting a new or modified vehicle is a wider question than demonstrating one repaired function. Use the functional-check comparison to distinguish the physical arrangements, without reading its movement as a speed profile, braking assessment or complete commissioning programme.

The handover connects work with operation

ORR’s public explanation distinguishes maintenance delivery and its release documentation from fleet-maintenance management’s return-to-operation role. That is a useful boundary for this teaching model, even where another jurisdiction uses different terms. The finished task, the supporting evidence and any relevant restrictions belong in the handover. Fleet allocation then connects the vehicle with an operational need, while railway control deals with the movement itself. Follow the links from a test fixture to the maintenance record, work-planning desk and departure road to see these different responsibilities. None of the atlas’s animations issues a release or authorizes a railway movement.

Read the complete electrification chain

Collection, conversion and return are separate design choices. Compare four complete teaching arrangements while keeping propulsion independent.

Compare collection and return separately

Start with Fourth rail · DC, then select Third rail · DC. Both use a conductor rail and wayside rectification, but their normal traction-return arrangements differ. The fourth-rail example has separate supply and return shoes and conductors; the third-rail example returns through wheel connections and the running rails. The Railway Engineering Institution’s public electrification chapter explains this distinction. The paired side-contact geometry is an original teaching arrangement, not a reproduction of an installed railway.

Network Rail · Railway Engineering Institution (formerly PWI) · Siemens Mobility

A pantograph does not identify the supply type

Choose Overhead · DC, then Overhead · AC. Both use a contact wire and pantograph. The DC example retains wayside rectification, while the selected conventional AC chain introduces an onboard transformer and line converter before the DC link and motor inverter. Siemens’s contact-line overview discusses both DC and AC applications. Its AC supply overview and ABB’s conventional vehicle architecture help locate the conversion stages; neither source supplies the geometry or equipment positions used here.

Siemens Mobility · Siemens Mobility · ABB · Siemens Mobility

Keep the transformer’s circuits and the drive choice separate

In the AC example, the pantograph supplies the transformer’s primary circuit and the running rails provide its return relationship. The transformer secondary feeds the line converter, DC link and motor inverter through a separate circuit. Amber, cyan and copper traces distinguish these relationships; they are not one wire passing through the transformer or a plot of instantaneous AC current direction. Open the enclosure to inspect the conversion stages. The selected LIM or rotary propulsion remains an independent choice: follow the inverter to the appropriate motor mechanism rather than assuming that a pantograph determines the drive.

ABB · Indian Railways — CAMTECH · Siemens Mobility · Railway Technical Research Institute

Use the comparison to locate the next question

These arrangements expose where collection, conversion and return differ. They do not prescribe voltage ratings, protection settings, section transitions, neutral sections, bonding, clearances or an isolation method. The AC example uses the conventional architecture discussed by ABB, without adopting the experimental transformer also described in that article. A selected combination is not evidence of a commissioned commercial configuration. Use the linked substation, guideway and vehicle views to examine equipment at a different scale, then consult the public sources for their defined scope.

Separate wheel rotation from vehicle response

Demand, wheel torque, contact conditions and vehicle travel are connected, but they are not the same observation.

Begin with the two motion cues

The axle carries a rim marker while a separate marker follows its centre against a fixed reference. Animate rolling, spin and slide, or move the phase slider. The centre follows the same authored path so the wheel’s different rotation is easy to compare. These rates are illustrative, without mass, inertia, adhesion coefficients or a force calculation. The scene concerns a rotary axle drive and friction braking. It does not transfer those traction relationships to the LIM, whose thrust is developed through a reaction rail.

RSSB · Railway Technical Research Institute

Inspect two different interventions

Wheel-slide protection modulates brake effort; sanding introduces material at the wheel–rail interface. The protection comparison changes the actuator cue and wheel rotation. The sanding comparison instead exposes a reservoir, hose, nozzle and grains arriving ahead of the contact. Knorr-Bremse’s public equipment descriptions distinguish these mechanisms, and RSSB’s research discusses low adhesion and mitigation. The model does not adopt a supplier’s performance figures or implement a real controller. Sand appearing at the rail is not proof that a particular braking performance has been restored.

RSSB · Knorr-Bremse · Knorr-Bremse

Connect response with measurement and maintenance

An axle sensor reports rotation. The independent travel cue represents the separate question of how the vehicle is moving; it is not a particular sensor installation. Use the connected concepts to examine localization and the depot wheelset. A discrepancy can prompt investigation, but this scene supplies no diagnostic threshold, wheel-damage prediction or maintenance acceptance criterion. A requested effort, an observed motion and an accepted condition need their own evidence.

From infrastructure observation to follow-up evidence

Track, ground, drainage and structures meet in one location. Work on one interface does not close every observation there.

Read the support and water paths

The section places track on an earthwork beside a culvert and a small bridge. The formation carries the track support relationship; the culvert and outfall provide a separate water path. Network Rail’s public explanations connect slope condition and drainage, while its inspection example shows why some spaces need more than a view from track level. The geometry here is fictional. It contains no calculated earth pressure, water capacity, structural load or failure threshold.

Network Rail · Network Rail · Network Rail

Inspect, intervene, then check

Inspection shows a probe at the culvert and a marker at a bridge bearing. Work in progress adds a cleaning hose and removes the visible drain obstruction. Work complete removes the tool while leaving an open follow-up entry. Check recorded adds a separate inspection result for the drainage location. These are chosen states, not a work method or a timed repair sequence. The fixed boundary remains in place throughout. Its appearance conveys a distinct work location, without demonstrating track protection or permission to enter.

Network Rail · Crossrail Learning Legacy

Preserve the other question

The bearing observation remains visible after the drainage work and follow-up entry. It is a useful reminder to ask which asset and condition a piece of evidence covers. A repaired drain does not establish the condition of a nearby structure, and a recorded inspection does not automatically authorize the return of a route to service. Follow the record connection into the Configuration & change process to examine the identified subject, matching evidence and unresolved conditions. Worksite handback addresses a separate boundary.

Trace the dependencies behind a resilient service

An alternate data path helps only within the functions and dependencies that it actually covers.

Name the function before discussing redundancy

Two applications support fictional station information and power supervision. The communication paths are separate from their shared power bus, operator identity, configuration and recording. Select Path A lost: station information retains its alternate conduit, while power supervision loses its illustrated connection. Select Shared power lost: neither live service trace remains. The field equipment stays physically present in both comparisons. This is a dependency study, without an inference that equipment would automatically transfer between paths.

NIST · ENISA

Distinguish access, live information and history

Identity unavailable retains the field-indication path but removes the new operator-request connection. Recorder unavailable retains live interfaces while interrupting the record branch. These are selected functional boundaries of the fictional example, not universal behavior for sessions or railway control systems. ENISA’s railway report provides the context of asset groups and connecting conduits. The illustration provides no actual network address, access rule, software weakness or attack demonstration.

NIST · ENISA

Restore evidence as well as a connection

NIST’s published 2023 Revision 3 discusses recovery of OT state, data, configuration and programs. Here, Restored, unchecked reconnects the conduit while retaining a configuration mismatch and recording gap. Evidence checked adds separate checks without filling that gap. The comparison supplies no recovery time, synchronized replica or authorization to operate. Open the Configuration & change process to examine why the record, observed configuration and supporting evidence must be related to the same subject.

Follow access through the whole passenger journey

A usable route connects physical passage, understandable information, assistance and the boarding interface.

Inspect the connected interfaces

Begin at the street, pass the wide fare gate and follow the near lift to the platform. The tactile strip, display and help point are distinct equipment; their information links are not passenger paths. The ERA application guide connects obstacle-free routes with changes of level, identification and other station interfaces. It is EU guidance rather than a universal rulebook. This model specifies no compliant width, gradient, contrast, illumination or platform gap.

European Union Agency for Railways

Change the journey when a facility is unavailable

Lift unavailable stops the highlighted route before the near lift and exposes a service message and assistance connection. The stairs remain, but the step-free route is not redirected onto them. Alternate lift selects a different approach through the fictional station and preserves the original outage marker. TransLink’s public guidance connects elevator availability with journey planning and assistance. No real station layout, current outage or operator detour has been copied into this example.

TransLink

Continue from the platform into the train

Boarding aid needed retains a visible gap and stops the route at the platform. Aid in place adds a bridging plate and extends the trace through the doorway. Reaching the platform and being able to board are separate questions. RNIB’s public research summary identifies barriers involving ticketing, assistance, information, physical design and disruption. That evidence supports considering the whole journey, rather than treating a lift as a complete accessibility solution. It does not represent every passenger’s needs or validate the modeled route.

Match a changed item with its evidence

Use the Configuration & change process to distinguish the proposed change, observed configuration, matching evidence and next handover question.

Identify the subject before following the process

The two-dimensional map begins with an affected baseline and keeps proposed, recorded and observed states separate. The subject may be equipment, software, data or documentation. INCOSE’s public competency framework describes configuration identification, change control, status and audit as related responsibilities. The atlas turns those themes into an original learning map; it does not reproduce an INCOSE process or prescribe a railway’s governance. Select a step to inspect its inputs, contributing roles, action, outputs and review question.

INCOSE

Examine the matching evidence

The verification step receives the observed configuration, a verification question, results and exceptions. It asks whether the evidence concerns the correct item, interfaces and intended use. For example, relabelling a report from version A does not establish its applicability to version B. The relevant question is which evidence applies and where coverage or discrepancies remain unresolved. The diagram’s return to implementation keeps a mismatch visible instead of treating forward navigation as successful completion. IRSE’s public testing-and-commissioning abstract and Crossrail’s public certification-package guidance provide context for configuration and evidence traceability; the paid IRSE paper and project forms are not reproduced.

IRSE Australasian Section · Crossrail Learning Legacy

Keep reconciliation and handover boundaries explicit

Reconciliation connects the actual configuration, its records and the evidence while retaining conditions. It supplies information for a subsequent acceptance or handover question. Asset handover, maintenance release, worksite handback and a duty handover address different recipients and responsibilities, so they have their own maps. An owner label identifies a representative contributor and does not appoint that role as the approver. Reviewing a step in this atlas grants no authority to operate, move a train or enter a worksite. Public operator and regulator examples retain their jurisdiction and scope.

Read a station from boarding edge to equipment room

Start with physical places, then distinguish motion, sensing and returned information.

Keep the physical boundary explicit

An open edge, a lower barrier and a tall facade have visibly different geometry. A lesson about end access should preserve that choice. ST Engineering supplies examples of several barrier heights; the atlas selects two original forms for comparison. Trainway sensing is a separate choice: the LiDAR and paired-radar examples replace one another. A sensor is not a physical barrier, and neither the rendered volume nor its dimensions validate coverage.

Watch the mechanism before reading the indication

The boarding sequence connects the drive to the leaves and keeps the platform-facing and opposite-side train doors distinct. With a barrier fitted, pause after the leaves return. Locate different sensing areas

An object on the trainway, an object between train and facade, a closing-edge obstruction and access past an end gate occupy different spaces. The interspace example requires a facade. The gate example keeps the edge unchanged and shows its own hinge, latch and position contact. A report leaves the physical object or open gate in place; a camera supplies additional information at a separate interface.

Siemens Mobility · Portalp Railway · Wabtec · Molinari Sensors

Connect the passenger levels

The station study places stairs and the lift between a platform and concourse. The moving cabin has its own doors; separate landing assemblies stay with the building. In the authored trip, the car closes, travels through an opening in the concourse, aligns with the upper floor and opens there. The equipment room sits on that concourse with an access opening and service aisle, while brackets connect passenger devices to supporting structure. These choices make the scene legible without claiming a usable station design.

Six boundaries hidden inside the word handover

Learn which subject, evidence and responsibility is changing before drawing a process.

Start with the subject

A train can be physically complete but awaiting a technical question. An asset can be in use while some project responsibilities continue. A fault can be acknowledged while the condition remains. These are useful starting points for reading railway processes: ask what state is actually being described and whose question it answers. The six maps in this guide are original learning structures. Each names a subject, representative contributors, information entering and leaving the conversation, and a question that prevents two different states being confused. They do not provide a railway’s approval workflow or operating instructions.

Australian Rail Track Corporation · Frequentis

Configuration and change

INCOSE’s public competency framework places identification, controlled change, status and audit within configuration management. The corresponding learning map asks whether the changed item and its records still agree. A fictional module with a different connector is a useful example: the hardware observation, interface definition and test subject must refer to the same intended configuration. The IRSE public fleet case abstract provides a railway example of the need to connect testing, configuration verification and return to operation. Only that abstract is used here; its detailed process is not copied. A decision about a proposed change and evidence about an implemented change remain separate questions.

INCOSE · IRSE Australasian Section

Asset handover is a lifecycle interface

ARTC describes readiness across a project, with operations and maintenance needs connected to commissioning and handover. Metrolinx’s public overview separately identifies in-service information, handover records and asset-register updates. These examples explain why the receiving organization matters. In the learning map, a recipient needs an identifiable asset, usable information and a clear account of remaining conditions. The diagram does not assign contractual ownership or appoint an approver. Its useful output is a better question: can the people who inherit the responsibility identify what they are receiving and where its supporting information will be maintained?

Australian Rail Track Corporation · Metrolinx

Worksite handback concerns a different boundary

A worksite handback relates work-side information to the relevant operational-control arrangement. The public RailSafe example connects infrastructure condition, restrictions and communication with network control. The educational map stops at those relationships: it supplies no order for removing protection, restoring power, testing signalling or moving a train. Completing one discipline’s task can leave another interface unresolved. A work record, an understood restriction and an operational permission should therefore remain distinct in the reader’s mental model. Other organizations may use “handback” for different transfers, so the page states which meaning is being explored.

Sydney Trains / Transport for NSW RailSafe · Australian Rail Industry Standards Organisation

Maintenance delivery, fleet readiness and duty continuity

ORR’s maintenance-function explanation distinguishes technical delivery and its release documentation from fleet-maintenance management’s return-to-operation function. The maintenance map follows that information towards a proposed allocation, while keeping the subsequent movement-control interface separate. Duty handover has a different subject again: people need continuity of task-relevant information. HSE describes preparation, two-way exchange and incoming cross-checking. In that map, an outstanding item remains outstanding after the duty holder changes. Neither a completed form nor a new person makes the physical condition disappear.

Office of Rail and Road · Health and Safety Executive

Coordination continues while evidence develops

Incident coordination brings reports and responsible teams together. It is often better understood through parallel interfaces than through a single row of steps. The map therefore separates operational, passenger and technical questions and brings their updates back to a shared record. Acknowledgement is attention; coordination is an organized relationship between responsibilities; resolution needs its own evidence. For a graduate entering the industry, follow a real component link from any map, then return and ask who needs its information, what the information establishes, and which decision is still outside that component’s responsibility.

Frequentis · Health and Safety Executive

People, automation and train-control families

Understand what GoA changes without confusing a supplier, a radio or a staffing model with an operating function.

Begin with responsibilities

The role cards describe functions that a railway needs to allocate, rather than an organization chart or a set of staffing numbers. A person may perform several functions; another railway may distribute the same functions across several teams or locations. Traffic coordination, signalling control, power supervision, passenger support and technical maintenance need different information and produce different outputs. Reading the boundary on each card is as useful as reading its responsibilities: a service plan, a received indication, a maintenance record and a movement authority do not establish the same thing.

IRSE Netherlands · Siemens Mobility · Office of Rail and Road

GoA describes train-operating allocation

The automation comparison follows the ERTMS Users Group’s public explanation of GoA1 to GoA4. Manual driving, automatic driving with a driver, driverless operation with an onboard operating role, and unattended capability describe different allocations. They do not identify one signalling product. In particular, GoA4 capability removes reliance on an onboard driver or operating attendant for the defined routine operation; it does not mean that every person disappears from the train or railway. Degraded operation, recovery and the boundary between operating modes still need defined arrangements.

ERTMS Users Group · Office of Rail and Road

Passenger and field responsibilities remain visible

ORR’s public GoA4 guidance addresses passenger communication, emergency interfaces, depot operation and control-centre responsibilities alongside automated train operation. A dated Community of Metros research summary also reports that some GoA4-capable metros chose to carry attendants for other purposes, including customer service. These sources support a careful distinction between technical capability and the chosen operating model. They do not support a universal claim that platform attendants will be removed or that a particular percentage of staff can be eliminated. Assistance, accessibility, local conditions and the railway’s responsibilities remain questions to examine.

Office of Rail and Road · Community of Metros / Imperial College Railway and Transport Strategy Centre

Keep families, functions and suppliers separate

The train-control map offers conventional signalling, CBTC and ETCS/ERTMS as parallel learning routes. Protection, automatic operation, supervision, route control and detection are functions that help explain those routes. ATC is an umbrella term whose exact use varies; it should not stand for one supplier. ETCS is not a subtype of CBTC, and ATO can be considered separately over ETCS. Supplier examples then show how functions are implemented: SelTrac, Trainguard MT and Urbalis are named examples, not interchangeable diagrams. Historical SelTrac material may name Thales; Hitachi Rail’s acquisition notice explains the current supplier lineage.

Prover · ERTMS Users Group · European Commission, Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport · European Commission, Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport · Alstom · Siemens Mobility · Hitachi Rail

A device can belong in several explanations

A track circuit or axle counter answers a detection question. A balise or other reference device supplies information with a defined meaning in its system. A radio transports messages. Those equipment questions cut across the navigation tree, so links to shared devices should preserve the same component identity. Start with the family overview, inspect the relevant device, then return to the functional relationship. That route helps a newcomer understand why similar-looking hardware does not make two architectures equivalent.

Read a communications system from endpoint to endpoint

Begin with a person or a physical condition, locate the equipment, and distinguish the information from the action it may support.

Start with a service and its locations

A communications drawing becomes easier to read when the endpoints are named before the network is drawn. A passenger speaking at a help point, a position contact in a plant room, a crew member using a cab radio and a camera producing video are different sources. Their recipients also differ: an assigned answering role, a supervisory application, an operational fixed terminal or a video recorder. The Locations & connections view therefore changes the service as well as its equipment. Its train, wayside, station and head-end places are teaching categories. They are not four mandatory rooms, a real route layout or a claim that all services use the same transport network.

Moxa · Transport for NSW · Network Rail · Zenitel

Separate passive connections, active equipment and supply

The station rack brings several boundaries close enough to inspect. Installed fibre terminates at a passive panel. A patch lead reaches an optical module at a powered switch. A routing interface connects network scopes, while a supply or UPS supports electrical continuity. Opening and separating these assemblies answers a different question from tracing information in Connections: what physical object could be inspected or replaced? The onboard alternative then changes the physical setting. It distinguishes local device connections from an inter-consist backbone. Its rugged modules and vehicle sections are original geometry, without a vendor port layout, network address plan or assumed train-control safety function.

Westermo · Westermo · Moxa · ABB

Read SCADA in both directions

A field condition does not appear on an HMI without acquisition and communications. The status example shows a damper position, its contact, an input module, a local controller and the downstream presentation. The command example adds a separately visible output interface. It keeps the operator request, relay state, physical movement and returned indication distinct. Their invented delays make the relationships inspectable, but do not implement local permissives or protection. Stale indication is a selected comparison: the physical equipment and a last-known display disagree while quality is visibly impaired. The field state must not be inferred from the mere survival of a screen or network cabinet.

Transport for NSW · Siemens · Siemens Mobility · Health and Safety Executive

Keep voice and passenger outputs purposeful

A help point has transducers and call electronics, while its answering service has call state and an assigned recipient. The model presses a real button before showing a pending and then answered example. It does not promise a response time. Operational radio has a different access path, including cab equipment, an antenna and radio infrastructure. Its voice relationship is separate from train-control messages. Passenger information similarly distinguishes the source, local player and screen. PA adds a further physical boundary: an amplifier converts an audio service into power for a loudspeaker circuit. The moving cone explains a driver relationship; it says nothing about speech intelligibility or emergency priorities.

Zenitel · Network Rail · Televic Rail · Bosch Building Technologies · Zenitel

Distinguish observation from control and proof

Camera optics, a video stream, recording storage and a viewing client are different pieces of a video system. An available live image does not establish that a recording exists, and neither proves track clearance or electrical isolation. Access control makes another useful distinction. The relay and bolt can change while the door remains closed. The contact changes when the leaf actually moves, and that measurement can then reach a security application. The demonstration deliberately separates these states. It provides no credential scheme, escape design or authorization to enter a railway work area. In each view, ask which object supplies the information, what its recipient can infer, and what independent evidence is still needed.

Separate the technology choices

Collection, electrical supply, propulsion and train control are distinct choices. Four selected arrangements compare third-rail DC, fourth-rail DC, overhead DC and overhead AC, including the normal return path and conversion equipment. The initial fictional arrangement pairs LIM propulsion with loop-based SelTrac control. Compare a rotary drive without changing the control medium, or loop and radio control without changing the motor. These are teaching examples, not assertions of commissioned combinations.

The LIM reaction rail is a passive electromagnetic secondary. The inductive cable is a communication medium. DC conductors supply traction energy. Operational voice and passenger communications can use radio even when train control uses a track loop.

Dedicated conventional-signalling, ETCS and supplier-generation studies show their named architectures. An ETCS level does not select an electrification supply or a motor type. Compare platform sensing and platform doors in the platform view.

The connected railway

Places, vehicles and systems come together to provide a railway service.

Inspect the equipment →

Track & guideway

Running rail: head, web and foot

A shaped steel beam carries the wheel contact and passes its load into the track supports.

In a flat-bottom rail, the head provides the running surface, the web connects the section, and the broad foot meets the rail seat and restraints. Commercial profiles have different shapes and section properties.

The rail bridges adjacent supports. A wheel load therefore reaches several support points through bending, rather than dropping only into the sleeper directly beneath it. This is the load-path interpretation used in the model.

Wheel guidance also depends on the wheel and rail profiles together. The running rail is mechanically distinct from a traction conductor or a LIM reaction rail, even where they appear alongside it.

The stylized section, rail spacing and wheel profile are explanatory geometry, not a selected rail standard or a contact-stress calculation.

British Steel

Inspect the equipment →
Ballasted track

Rails and sleepers sit in a granular support bed, forming a layered mechanical system.

Ballasted track combines running rails, their fastenings, sleepers and a bed of stone. The ballast supports the sleepers and helps preserve the track's geometry.

The model follows the load through this assembly: wheel to rail, rail seat to sleeper, then through the stone bed into the prepared foundation. Each layer has a different role; ballast is not a replacement for the fastening that holds the rail.

A cutaway makes the distinction visible: the rail is restrained locally at repeated seats, while the granular bed supports and surrounds the sleeper.

Layer depths, sleeper spacing and ballast shoulders are illustrative. This comparison does not select a track design for a particular railway.

Network Rail

Inspect the equipment →
Ballast: support and drainage

The stone bed distributes load, restrains sleepers and provides connected spaces for drainage.

Ballast transfers sleeper loads through contacts between particles. Material around the sleeper also contributes lateral restraint, so the bed's function extends beyond vertical cushioning.

The spaces between particles provide drainage paths. Research on fouled ballast shows that fine material can fill these spaces, retain water and reduce the bed's ability to pass water.

Load transmission and drainage therefore use the same physical layer in different ways: forces travel through the particle contacts, while water travels through the connected voids. The model separates these two paths visually.

Particle size, fouling level and water animation are qualitative; the scene does not predict drainage capacity or track settlement.

Mid-America Transportation Center / University of Kansas

Inspect the equipment →
Subballast and separation layer

An intermediate layer separates ballast from the foundation and spreads load.

Subballast sits between ballast and subgrade. Its functions include distributing load, limiting the mixing of adjacent materials and directing water toward drainage.

Its role differs from the open stone bed above. The model uses a finer layer and lateral drainage path to make that distinction visible.

Materials and drainage arrangements vary; the historical reference is not a current design specification.

Federal Railroad Administration / US Department of Transportation

Inspect the equipment →
Formation and subgrade

The prepared foundation forms the largely hidden end of the track's load path.

The subgrade is the soil or other foundation material beneath the track layers. Its support and drainage behavior affect the structure built above it.

In this model, formation means the prepared upper foundation surface. A simplified soft-support animation demonstrates why sound rails alone cannot ensure stable geometry when their underlying support deforms.

Terminology varies. Deformation is illustrative, without a soil or settlement calculation.

Federal Railroad Administration / US Department of Transportation

Inspect the equipment →
Sleeper or tie

A sleeper carries repeated rail seats, maintains their relationship and spreads forces into the support below.

Sleepers anchor the rails through their fastenings and transfer forces to the track substructure. Their geometry and materials are selected for the loading and environment.

The concrete sleeper shown here has two rail seats. These seats and their fastenings keep the rails in the intended lateral relationship while the sleeper distributes their loads over a larger supporting area.

An optional under-sleeper pad lies beneath the sleeper and changes its contact with ballast. It is a different component from the rail pad directly beneath a rail foot.

Concrete is one sleeper material, not a universal choice. The model does not reproduce prestressing details or a structural reinforcement design.

Vossloh

Inspect the equipment →
Rail pad and resilient layer

An elastic layer between rail and support changes how wheel forces and vibration enter the track structure.

A rail pad sits beneath the rail foot at the support. In resilient fastenings, elastomeric pads allow controlled deflection and influence how vertical forces reach the supporting structure.

Changing the pad changes the support's force–deflection behavior. It can also change vibration transmission; the rail, fasteners and structure still act as a connected system.

The model exaggerates a small pad compression so its role becomes visible. It does not treat stiffness and damping as the same quantity or imply that the softest pad is automatically the best choice.

No pad stiffness, damping coefficient or predicted noise reduction is assigned. The animation is qualitative.

Vossloh

Inspect the equipment →
Elastic rail clip and shoulder

A spring element presses the rail into its seat while its anchor transfers restraint to the support.

An elastic rail fastening combines a spring clip with anchorage and contact components. The clip's elastic deflection produces a retaining force on the rail foot.

In the selected example, a shoulder anchors the clip, an insulator separates a contact interface, and a pad supports the rail. These components cooperate to restrain the rail while permitting the fastening's intended elastic movement.

The clip is therefore more than a decorative curved bracket. Its shape and constrained contact points make it a spring, while the shoulder gives that spring a mechanical reaction point.

Clip shapes, anchors and assembly arrangements differ. This is a functional model, without tightening, insertion or inspection instructions.

Pandrol

Inspect the equipment →
Rail-seat insulator

A small interface component can contribute both electrical separation and lateral positioning.

Rail fastenings can include insulating components at restraint interfaces. These separate conducting parts while transmitting mechanical contact forces.

Insulator geometry also matters mechanically: in some fastening families, changing the side component changes the rail's lateral position. The model shows that such a piece is part of the rail-seat geometry, not simply a colored electrical symbol.

One insulating piece does not establish whole-track insulation or define traction return.

Pandrol

Inspect the equipment →
Baseplate and rail seat

A plate organizes the rail support, restraints and attachment to the structure beneath it.

A baseplate can carry the rail pad and fastening components on timber, composite or concrete supports. Different plate arrangements connect the same basic rail-seat functions to different foundations.

Some assemblies add resilience below the plate as well as below the rail. Separating those two levels explains why a fastening can have several layers without each layer being another rail pad.

Plate count, resilience and attachment vary; this stack is illustrative.

Pandrol

Inspect the equipment →
Direct-fixation track

Individual rail supports attach to a structural base while retaining engineered resilience and restraint.

Direct fixation attaches rail-support assemblies to a slab or other structural support without an intervening ballast bed. The assembly can include a baseplate, anchors, resilient intermediate layers and electrical insulation.

The word direct describes the support arrangement. It does not mean that the rail must be rigidly fastened against bare concrete: the rail and plate can still deflect through their resilient layers.

In this model, wheel forces pass through the rail seat and fastening into the concrete support. The distinct mechanical and electrical interfaces remain visible in the cutaway.

Anchor layout, embedment and layer thickness are schematic. The scene is not a fastening selection or an anchorage design.

Vossloh

Inspect the equipment →
Slab track

A concrete structural layer supports the rail system in place of the conventional ballast bed.

Slab track is a family of constructions rather than one universal stack. One established approach combines precast rail-support blocks with a cast-in-place concrete track slab.

The structural slab and the rail support are different levels of the assembly. Concrete provides the supporting structure; the selected rail fastening supplies the local restraint and resilience.

The comparison model offers separate construction presets: embedded support blocks in a slab, or individual direct-fixation seats on concrete. Showing them separately avoids presenting components from different systems as one mandatory design.

Slab reinforcement, joints, foundations and durability provisions require project-specific design. No maintenance-free claim is made.

RAILONE

Inspect the equipment →
Concrete plinth

A raised concrete support places direct fasteners above the underlying slab or deck.

A plinth can take the form of a longitudinal concrete block supporting direct rail fasteners. It transfers forces into the underlying structure and establishes a support level above it.

The rail's final position follows the combined geometry of the structural support, plinth and fastening assembly. The plinth is therefore distinct from the small baseplate immediately below the rail seat.

In the section model, the plinth connects a close-up fastening assembly to the much larger guideway deck. This makes the change in structural scale visible without adopting a real installation's dimensions.

Plinth form and attachment depend on the structure and track design. No tolerances, repair method or construction sequence is provided.

Eungcheol Kim, Myungseob Kim, Gabrielle Delos and Tyler Clark / Sustainability

Inspect the equipment →
Embedded rail

A rail can receive continuous elastic support inside a channel rather than repeated exposed rail seats.

Embedded systems can surround the rail with resilient profiles or compounds that provide continuous vertical and lateral support. This differs from a rail held at widely separated sleeper seats.

The surrounding elastic system can also contribute vibration isolation and electrical separation. Embedded construction is therefore more than placing bare steel directly in concrete.

The street-context model removes a slice of paving to reveal the rail, resilient surround and supporting channel. The running surface and the wheel-flange path remain open; the exact exposed profile depends on the selected construction.

The street scene is a support-system comparison, not an exposed conductor-rail or LIM street-running design.

Inspect the equipment →
Turnout: one track to two routes

A turnout combines a movable switch, connecting rails and a crossing into one route-changing assembly.

The switch selects the entry path; closure rails connect that region to the crossing, or frog, where the rail paths intersect. These are distinct parts of the complete turnout.

The model follows a wheelset along either route. Route selection changes the switch geometry at the entry; it does not rotate every rail or move the fixed frog.

Geometry is illustrative; no permitted speed or route authorization is implied.

voestalpine Railway Systems / Nortrak-Damy

Inspect the equipment →
Stock rail

The fixed rail provides the mating surface beside a movable switch rail.

At a switch, the stock rail and the tapered switch rail have coordinated contact geometry. Their relationship guides the wheel through the transition into the selected path.

In this model the stock rail stays fixed. A closing blade approaches its mating face, making the distinction between the stationary rail and the moving route-selection component explicit.

Simplified mating profiles are not a manufacturer's geometry or machining drawing.

voestalpine Railway Systems

Inspect the equipment →
Switch rail or blade

A tapered movable rail changes which continuous wheel path is available through the switch.

A switch rail narrows toward its tip so its contact geometry can meet the stock rail and guide the wheel onto the chosen path.

The selected model uses flexible blades: one closes toward a stock rail as the other opens away. The animation emphasizes the changing contact relationship rather than treating the complete rail as a short rigid door hinge.

Flexible blades are one example; actual movement and locking architectures differ.

voestalpine Railway Systems

Inspect the equipment →
Closure rail

Connecting rails carry the running paths from the switch region toward the crossing.

Closure rails join the switch and frog within the turnout. They complete the connecting geometry between the route-selection region and the crossing.

In the model these rails remain fixed while the blades move. Their curvature and alignment make the selected wheel path continuous; they are not additional switch blades simply because they lie inside the turnout.

Joins and curvature are schematic, without fabrication dimensions.

voestalpine Railway Systems / Nortrak-Damy

Inspect the equipment →
Crossing or frog

A crossing lets one rail path pass through another while leaving space for wheel flanges.

A conventional fixed crossing includes a pointed vee, or nose, and wing rails around it. Flangeways provide passages through the intersecting rail geometry.

The wheel must pass from one supporting running surface to the next near this interruption. The model makes the nose, wing rails and flange passages visible instead of hiding them beneath a solid X-shaped block.

This is a fixed, tread-bearing example. Other crossing arrangements change the moving elements or the way the wheel is supported, so the same contact animation should not be applied to every frog type.

Flangeway dimensions and wheel-contact transitions are schematic. The scene does not calculate impact loads or wear.

voestalpine Railway Systems

Inspect the equipment →
Check rail or crossing guard rail

A guide beside the opposite running rail helps position the wheelset as the other wheel passes the frog.

A conventional crossing guard rail lies on the gauge side of the running rail opposite the frog. Its guiding action helps keep the wheelset aligned and protects the crossing nose.

The key relationship spans the axle: guiding one wheel helps position the wheel at the crossing on the other side. A single-wheel animation would hide this relationship.

The illustrated guide works against the inner back face of the wheel when contact is needed. It is not an extra normal tread-support rail, an electrical conductor or a LIM reaction rail.

Check-rail and guard-rail terminology varies. Derailment-containment rails elsewhere on the railway can serve a different purpose.

voestalpine Railway Systems Nortrak

Inspect the equipment →
Stretcher bar and blade linkage

A mechanical link coordinates the relationship between the two switch rails.

A stretcher bar connects switch rails so their positions remain related: one side can be closed while the other is open. The assembly includes the bar and its connecting parts.

Some arrangements include electrical insulation in the connection. That electrical separation does not remove the mechanical job of transmitting movement and maintaining the intended blade relationship.

In the model the linkage is distinct from a sleeper, which supports the rails, and from a detector, which reports their position. Linking, supporting and sensing are different functions.

Bar count, attachment positions and joint construction are illustrative; the cited glossary supplies terminology rather than a design to reproduce.

Rail Accident Investigation Branch

Inspect the equipment →
Point machine and lock

A point-operating system moves the switch rails and provides the required locking function.

Point systems combine a drive with a locking arrangement; detection may be integrated or separate. Movement, retention and position reporting remain distinct functions.

The model uses a generic electromechanical example: a motor and transmission move a drive rod linked to the blades. A separate lock indicator explains why reaching a position and securing it are not the same action.

The cutaway is original illustrative geometry, without operating instructions.

Point-position detection

Feedback reports the physical switch state rather than merely repeating the requested route.

Point detectors check switch-rail positions and can form part of the locking and proving arrangement. Their task differs from the drive that moves the rails.

The teaching model separates a requested route from confirmed position. A command or a stopped motor alone is not treated as proof that the blades and locking arrangement have reached the required state.

This functional explanation supplies no signalling circuit, bypass or recovery sequence.

Inspect the equipment →
Crossover

Two connected turnouts allow a train to transfer between parallel tracks.

A crossover consists of a pair of turnouts joined between parallel tracks. The connection provides a route from one track to the other.

The model expands the single-turnout view to show both ends of that connecting route. A wheelset must follow compatible geometry through both turnouts, not merely cross a colored line between the tracks.

This differs from a diamond crossing: a plain diamond lets two alignments intersect but does not, by itself, provide a transfer between them.

The layout is schematic. It does not state a railway's permitted direction of travel, operating rules or signalling authorization.

Inspect the equipment →
Diamond crossing

Two tracks intersect at the same level while each continues along its own alignment.

A diamond places the rail intersections of two crossing tracks within one special-trackwork assembly. In a plain fixed diamond, the geometry does not select a transfer between the two alignments.

The wheel-support details matter at each intersection. Crossing products include different support arrangements, including flange-bearing alternatives, so there is no single contact animation that accurately describes every diamond.

The baseline model is a schematic fixed, tread-bearing example. It exposes the crossing gaps and guidance features while keeping the two through routes distinct.

The example is not a turnout, a road level crossing or a universal diamond design. No crossing angle or load capacity is specified.

A traction transformer transfers energy through a magnetic core between its winding circuits. Its place in the chain depends on the supply architecture: the DC substation feeds a rectifier, while a conventional AC train also has an onboard transformer.

Traction rectifier

A wayside diode rectifier supplies the selected DC profiles.

The selected DC substation converts the transformer output into a DC traction supply. This diode arrangement is one-way; regenerated energy is received elsewhere on the DC network or by the chosen resistor.

The dedicated assembly view separates clamped semiconductor devices, heat sinks, busbars and enclosure. The AC supply chain removes this wayside rectifier.

The electrical-principle view follows an ideal six-diode bridge for one three-phase cycle. The phase at the highest voltage feeds the positive bus; the lowest phase provides the return. The DC output has six ripple pulses per input cycle.

Wayside braking resistor

Turns surplus electrical energy into heat.

During electrical braking, the train can deliver energy back to the DC network. If receptive loads are unavailable, suitably controlled resistors can absorb energy instead.

Resistors may be onboard or trackside. The enclosure and cooling path matter because the removed kinetic energy becomes heat; a resistor is not an energy store.

Carbody and equipment zones

Houses people and the vehicle systems.

Bogie and wheelsets

Connect the carbody to the track.

Traction inverter / propulsion converter

Controls electrical power delivered to the motor.

A traction converter uses controlled power electronics to supply an AC motor. In the selected DC examples, it connects the conductor-rail supply to either the LIM primary or the rotary traction motors.

Its control, thermal management and protection work together. During electrical braking, compatible conversion equipment transfers generated energy back toward the DC supply.

“PCU” is a broad propulsion-control label, not a promise of identical hardware or naming across manufacturers.

LIM primary

Produces the motor’s travelling magnetic field.

The train-mounted primary carries the energized windings. Magnetic coupling across the air gap induces current in the conducting secondary; their interaction produces longitudinal force.

Direct electromagnetic thrust does not require the wheels to transmit propulsion torque. In this illustrated wheel-supported train, the LIM is not a levitation system.

Travelling field, slip and air gap

Relative motion makes induction possible.

The travelling field and secondary move relative to one another. In an idealized induction model, that relative speed sets the induced-current frequency; synchronous motion gives zero slip.

The air gap participates in the magnetic circuit. Changing gap or relative motion changes the interaction, but this visual model does not calculate a real motor’s force or efficiency.

Finite-length effects, saturation and thermal limits require a more complete machine model; no quantitative performance is inferred.

Blended braking and friction brakes

Several brake mechanisms cooperate to slow the train.

Brake control allocates the requested braking effort among available mechanisms. Electrical braking can recover energy; friction braking supplies additional or replacement effort when needed.

Wheel-slide protection monitors axle behaviour and adjusts braking effort when adhesion is limited. Braking performance depends on equipment, operating conditions and the selected control strategy.

Regenerative capability and brake blending vary across designs and operating conditions.

Holds a stationary vehicle.

Parking is a distinct function from continuous electrical braking. A spring-applied brake is one available implementation.

Where braking energy goes

Energy needs a destination.

Electrical braking converts some motion into electrical energy. A receptive network can use it elsewhere; otherwise suitable resistors can dissipate it as heat.

Compare a receptive train with wayside resistor dissipation. The animation shows energy destinations, not a recovery percentage or stopping-distance prediction.

The selected diode rectifier cannot send energy backward into the AC utility. Grid regeneration needs suitable reversible equipment.

Auxiliary conversion provides suitable power for onboard applications separately from traction-motor conversion. A battery charger may be integrated with the auxiliary converter.

Conditions the passenger environment.

Rotary traction motor

An electric motor develops torque that drives a wheelset in this selected arrangement.

The inverter supplies the motor with controlled electrical power. Its rotating electromagnetic field produces torque at a shaft; a coupling and gear unit transmit that torque to a driven axle. Wheel–rail adhesion then transfers the longitudinal force.

Compare this torque path with the LIM: the LIM primary exchanges electromagnetic force with a track-mounted reaction rail. The rotary example has a driven wheelset and does not need that LIM secondary. Either propulsion choice can be combined with a separately designed train-control system.

Original schematic geometry; this is one geared rotary drive, not a representation of every motor or bogie.

A gearbox is not a train-control computer. Changing the train-to-wayside communication medium does not add or remove this mechanical drive. Direct-drive and other mechanical arrangements also exist.
