Train control

Automatic train protection · ATP

Supervises movement limits and can demand braking.

ATP checks whether train movement remains inside its permitted envelope. ETCS provides one public example: onboard supervision compares position and speed with applicable limits, predicts the approach to a target, and can command brake intervention.

The protection computer issues a command; the vehicle braking equipment produces the physical force. In the teaching model, increasing an ATO driving request cannot raise the protection limit.

Specific supervision functions, margins and intervention rules depend on the system.

European Union Agency for Railways

Inspect the equipment →
Automatic train operation · ATO

Drives toward operational targets within protection constraints.

ATO calculates driving actions such as acceleration, coasting and braking from the journey target and the information available to it. In the published ATO-over-ETCS arrangement, timetable information arrives from an ATO trackside function, while onboard ATO interfaces with traction and brakes.

ETCS retains the protection responsibility and determines when ATO may operate. Automation grade also describes who performs tasks: automatic driving can coexist with a driver in the cab. Driverless operation brings additional operational and supervision requirements; selecting ATO alone does not establish them.

The example explains ATO over ETCS; metro implementations allocate interfaces differently.

ERTMS Users Group

Inspect the equipment →
Automatic train supervision · ATS

Coordinates the service across a line or network.

ATS gives controllers a network view and supports traffic regulation, timetable recovery, incident handling and service changes. A regulation decision might hold a train, adjust a departure or request a different service pattern. These are operating objectives that still pass through the applicable route and protection functions.

A control centre can also display traction-power SCADA, communications and security systems. Integration in one room or screen does not make those functions identical. Alstom publishes separate modules for these responsibilities, alongside its traffic-supervision and regulation tools.

Control-centre architecture and the scope of ATS vary by project.

Alstom

Inspect the equipment →
Onboard train-control computer

Connects train information, protection and driving functions.

An onboard control function reports train position and receives information governing movement. Mitsubishi Electric describes an arrangement exchanging these messages with a wayside zone controller, enabling automatic driving within the applicable speed restriction.

Our cabinet view separates localization, protection and driving responsibilities. Lines to the traction and brake systems represent commands and feedback, not the high-power path that supplies a motor.

Functional boxes do not specify the number of computers or their physical allocation.

Mitsubishi Electric

Inspect the equipment →
Train control and management system · TCMS

Coordinates vehicle equipment and reports its condition.

A TCMS connects commands, status and diagnostics across subsystems such as traction, braking, doors, lighting and HVAC.

Follow a driving request to the propulsion controller, then follow the status response back. This is a vehicle-management role; the diagram gives movement permission its own clearly labelled function.

Hardware integration and the TCMS boundary are supplier- and project-dependent.

Škoda Group

Inspect the equipment →
Wayside zone controller

Uses train reports to support control within an area.

In the example architecture, the zone controller receives train position reports and returns movement-related control information. The published Mitsubishi Electric arrangement addresses separation, speed and route control through exchanges between onboard and wayside equipment.

The model shows a report arriving before a response is delivered. A message contains information, not traction energy. Cabinet location, controller boundaries and the division of functions are implementation choices.

A zone-controller box is one architecture, not a universal CBTC requirement.

Mitsubishi Electric

Inspect the equipment →
Balise and onboard reader

Transfers localized track information as the train passes.

A Eurobalise is a track-mounted transponder energized by a passing train’s reader antenna. It provides a data telegram containing fixed or switchable information, such as a location reference or infrastructure data. The onboard balise transmission module processes the received message.

The train moves beyond the brief contact region and continues onboard supervision. A balise therefore is not a continuous radio access point, a wheel counter or a traction power source.

Eurobalise is the ETCS example; metro transponder functions and formats differ.

European Commission, Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport

Inspect the equipment →
Wheel-speed sensor · tachometer

Measures wheel rotation for motion estimation.

Wheel rotation estimates speed and distance using a wheel-size assumption.

A sliding wheel can misrepresent vehicle speed. Compare its estimate with independent information.

This wheel-supported LIM example demonstrates friction-braking wheel slide; propulsion force is developed by the linear motor.

German Aerospace Center (DLR), Oliver Heirich and Benjamin Siebler

Inspect the equipment →
Accelerometer and inertial measurement unit

Add an independent view of vehicle motion.

Acceleration and rotational measurements complement wheel-based odometry.

Integration accumulates error. Combining complementary measurements and position references can constrain drift; localization still retains uncertainty.

Sensor selection and estimation algorithms vary.

Deutsche Bahn — Digitale Schiene Deutschland · German Aerospace Center (DLR), Oliver Heirich and Benjamin Siebler

Inspect the equipment →
Brake controller and wheel-slide protection

Translate braking demand into coordinated braking action.

Brake control coordinates available brake systems and can account for vehicle load. Wheel-slide protection is one of its supporting functions.

A braking command and the resulting deceleration are different quantities. Sensors provide feedback; a command alone is not proof that the train has slowed.

Brake blending, assurance and emergency arrangements are system-specific.

Knorr-Bremse

Inspect the equipment →
Communications-based train control · CBTC

Uses frequent train information to support movement control.

A contemporary radio CBTC arrangement combines onboard localization, train-to-wayside communication and control functions that supervise movements. The useful information is the train state and movement permission carried by the messages; the radio link is the transport mechanism.

CBTC is a family of architectures. Alstom explicitly describes moving-block and optimized fixed-block approaches, different automation grades and newer train-centric allocations. This site uses a wayside-controller example to make the responsibilities visible, then lets you compare alternatives without implying that every installation uses the same boxes.

CBTC is neither a propulsion type nor a synonym for unattended operation.

Alstom

Inspect the equipment →
Movement authority

Defines permission to move within stated limits.

A movement authority permits a train to proceed to a specified location subject to infrastructure constraints. It must be interpreted with the applicable speed and track information. In ETCS, an end of authority is a location associated with a zero target speed.

The teaching display uses an endpoint and a permitted-speed ribbon. A driving request cannot extend either one. Authority, actual train position and the requested timetable are therefore three separate objects.

The ribbon is conceptual and does not reproduce a protocol or certified calculation.

ERA, UNISIG and ERTMS Users Group

Inspect the equipment →
Interlocking

Checks and secures compatible routes through the railway.

An interlocking evaluates the information needed before a route can be used: track-section status, point position and the required signalling conditions. It coordinates points and signals so a route request becomes a controlled movement rather than merely a command to move switch blades.

Electronic interlockings exchange commands and indications with field equipment, sometimes through object controllers. The model separates a requested route, a proved route and a released route. A missing point indication or uncertain section state leaves the route unproved in this example.

Route locking and release rules are project-specific; the sequence is illustrative.

Siemens Mobility

Inspect the equipment →
Point machine, lock and detector

Moves switch blades and reports the resulting condition.

A point operating system changes the route through a turnout. Its drive moves the switch blades, locking equipment restrains the required position, and detection checks the resulting blade or lock condition. Siemens publishes arrangements with separate locks, detector rods and end-position detectors.

These functions may occupy different housings or be combined. An animation of a moving rod only demonstrates actuation. The route model should wait for a separate proved indication before showing the switch as available for a train movement.

The geometry is a generic teaching arrangement, not an installation or adjustment guide.

Siemens Mobility

Inspect the equipment →
Track-section detection

Determines whether a defined section can be treated as clear.

A section detector supplies occupancy information to signalling. A basic track circuit uses an electrical condition of the running rails; an axle counter instead evaluates wheels passing section boundaries. Neither display should be confused with a continuously measured position for the front of a train.

The model distinguishes clear, occupied and unavailable information. When the nose crosses a boundary, the old section remains occupied while part of the train is still inside it.

Detector type, proving conditions and degraded procedures vary.

Network Rail · voestalpine Railway Systems

Inspect the equipment →
Track circuit

Uses the running rails in a section-detection circuit.

In a basic track circuit, a supply and receiver are connected through the rails. A wheelset electrically links the rails and changes the receiver condition, indicating occupation. The educational circuit therefore follows the running rails rather than the separate traction supply rail or LIM reaction rail.

Network Rail explains that faults can produce an occupied indication and restrict traffic. Real track circuits use different electrical arrangements; this simple relay sketch demonstrates the detection principle.

This diagram does not establish broken-rail detection capability or immunity to every failure.

Network Rail

Inspect the equipment →
Axle counter

Counts wheel passages at the edges of a section.

Trackside wheel sensors detect axle passages and direction. Evaluation equipment compares the events at the boundaries of the protected section to determine its occupancy state. The published voestalpine example includes monitored sensors and evaluation equipment for tracks and turnouts.

A balanced count is meaningful only within a valid evaluation state. The teaching model therefore shows count balance and information validity separately. It also distinguishes the wayside counter from an onboard tachometer: one supports section occupancy, while the other supplies wheel-motion information.

Counts in the demonstration are invented for teaching and are not recovery instructions.

voestalpine Railway Systems

Inspect the equipment →
Lineside signal and route indication

Presents movement instructions to a driver.

A lineside signal communicates an instruction or permission at a particular point. Colour-light signals may also have a route indication, helping a driver understand which path has been established. Network Rail distinguishes these visible signals from the broader system that detects trains, operates points and protects movements.

Some signalling arrangements present information inside the cab instead. A green-looking lamp alone is therefore an incomplete explanation of the railway: route establishment, detection and the applicable operating rules also matter. This model uses explicitly labelled stop and proceed indications rather than teaching a national aspect code.

Aspect meanings and driver obligations depend on the railway and its rulebook.

Network Rail

Inspect the equipment →
Fixed-block separation

Divides track into predetermined detection or signalling sections.

A fixed-block model uses boundaries that stay at defined places on the railway. The condition of the sections ahead constrains a following movement. When the leading train occupies part of a section, that section cannot simply be treated as empty space behind its front.

Stopping distance, observation or supervision, train length and margins all affect separation. Shortening a drawn block is not by itself proof that a real railway can safely run closer together.

The comparison omits operating exceptions and must not be used to determine headway.

University of Birmingham, Birmingham Centre for Railway Research and Education

Inspect the equipment →
Moving-block separation

Relates a following limit to the protected position of the train ahead.

A moving-block illustration lets the separation boundary change with the leading train rather than tying every limit to fixed section endpoints. Knowledge of train position and extent supports this approach; the following train still needs sufficient protected stopping space.

The benefit comes from using movement information differently, not from removing braking distance. The display retains a position-uncertainty region and a braking envelope while the leading train moves.

This is a conceptual comparison, not a capacity or certified-separation calculation.

University of Birmingham, Birmingham Centre for Railway Research and Education

Inspect the equipment →
Odometry and position estimation

Combines measured motion with known position references.

Odometry estimates speed and distance from motion sensors. Deutsche Bahn identifies pulse generators, radar and accelerometers as established examples; independent measurements can be combined. A known passing reference such as a balise supplies a different kind of information from the motion measured between references.

Our experiment labels the true distance as a known example reference and deliberately biases a synthetic wheel measurement. A second sensor and a reference update help explain why information is combined. They do not make every estimate exact or establish the performance of a real train. Newer localization research also investigates landmark and satellite measurements.

Sensor combinations and assurance methods differ; research demonstrations are not universal installed equipment.

Deutsche Bahn, Digitale Schiene Deutschland

Inspect the equipment →
Braking curve and target supervision

Predicts the speed reduction needed before a target.

A braking curve relates allowable or predicted speed to the distance remaining toward a target. ERA explains that ETCS builds its prediction from train braking dynamics and the track ahead, then uses that prediction in onboard supervision.

A toy slider can show why a poorer assumed deceleration needs more space. The resulting curve is an explanatory calculation only; certified braking models include detailed inputs and supervision rules that this site does not reproduce.

A service-braking animation is not evidence of an emergency-stop guarantee.

European Union Agency for Railways

Inspect the equipment →
Train integrity and protected rear position

Asks whether the complete train remains together.

Train integrity concerns confidence that the train is complete and has not left vehicles behind. A report of the leading end’s position answers a different question. To reason about the space occupied by a whole train, its extent and completeness also matter.

The illustration places separate markers on the front and rear and a distinct integrity-status badge. Changing the front position does not automatically clear the previous section or prove that the rear has followed.

Integrity assurance and trackside detection depend on the chosen architecture.

ERA, UNISIG and ERTMS Users Group

Inspect the equipment →
ETCS Level 1

Combines spot transmission with continuing onboard supervision.

Level 1 typically transfers trackside information through Eurobalises as the train passes. Onboard supervision continues between those transmissions, checking permitted speed and the approach to the end of movement authority.

In the basic view, interlocking information reaches a switchable balise through an LEU, while lineside signals and separate train detection remain visible. Infill arrangements can supply information before the next balise; the displayed base case omits them.

Intermittent communication does not mean intermittent protection.

European Commission, Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport

Inspect the equipment →
ETCS Level 2

Uses radio for continuing train–trackside exchanges.

Level 2 combines continuous onboard supervision with radio communication. The radio block centre and onboard equipment exchange movement information; balises still provide references. Lineside signals are optional in the architecture.

The Commission’s current overview incorporates the former Level 3 category into Level 2 under the 2023 CCS TSI. Detection and integrity may therefore be supplied by trackside equipment or managed within ERTMS, depending on the configuration.

Level 2 alone does not specify moving block, absence of signals or automation grade.

European Commission, Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport

Inspect the equipment →
Radio block centre · RBC

Provides ETCS movement information over radio.

An RBC receives reports from trains and sends movement authority and associated information. It interfaces with the interlocking and other ground functions; a radio tower by itself does not make the route-control decisions.

The model distinguishes the logical RBC, its communication path and the onboard receiver. The train’s EVC checks the received data and supervises movement locally. The response is therefore part of a distributed control arrangement, not remote steering of a traction inverter.

Physical hosting, interfaces and boundaries differ between implementations.

MERMEC Group

Inspect the equipment →
ETCS onboard equipment · EVC and DMI

Processes movement data, supervises the train and informs the driver.

The European Vital Computer applies the onboard protection logic using received information and train inputs such as odometry. Interfaces connect the protection function to relevant vehicle systems. A driver-machine interface presents indications and supports driver interaction.

These roles should remain visually distinct: the display is not the entire protection computer, and the computer is not the physical brake. The cutaway links reader, radio and motion inputs to the EVC, then separates its driver display from its train-control interface.

The diagram explains functions without reproducing a certified cab display or wiring arrangement.

MERMEC Group

Inspect the equipment →
Lineside electronic unit · LEU

Connects signalling information to a switchable Eurobalise.

An LEU receives information from the interlocking and supplies an appropriate telegram to a switchable Eurobalise. The balise then communicates that information to the passing train. A fixed-data balise illustrates a different use: its information is not being selected from the current route state.

The model places the LEU between the interlocking and the balise, making the source of the message visible instead of treating every track transponder as an isolated position marker.

This is an ETCS constituent, not a generic name for every wayside radio controller.

European Commission, Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport

Inspect the equipment →
Railway radio · GSM-R and FRMCS

Separates communication technology from the train-control application.

GSM-R adapted GSM technology for railway needs. FRMCS is its specified successor; UIC’s public 2025 system requirements describe a 5G-based system and interfaces through which railway applications use communications services. The radio system transports information for applications rather than replacing their signalling logic.

Migration is a coordinated change to equipment, networks and applications. UIC explicitly describes scenarios in which users attach to GSM-R, FRMCS or temporarily both. The comparison therefore shows coexistence, not a universal switchover date. A generic 5G metro deployment should not automatically be labelled FRMCS.

This educational view makes no claim about a particular network’s rollout schedule.

Inspect the equipment →
SelTrac · a published CBTC family

A supplier example with several generations and communication arrangements.

SelTrac belongs to Hitachi Rail’s urban signalling portfolio. Hitachi completed its acquisition of Thales’ Ground Transportation Systems business on 31 May 2024; older documents therefore carry a different supplier name.

Treat the family as a case study, with separately labelled historical and contemporary examples. The comparison does not assign one cabinet arrangement, radio bearer or propulsion system to every SelTrac deployment.

Brand and generation labels do not establish any particular installation’s configuration.

Hitachi Rail

Inspect the equipment →
Legacy SelTrac inductive-loop example

Uses a track loop as the local train–wayside communication medium.

Public 2009 planning material explicitly distinguishes an inductive-loop system from a proposed wayside-radio SelTrac upgrade. This is evidence of different communication arrangements, not a claim about when any particular migration was completed.

An archived public explanation describes very short-range wireless communication through a loop cable between the rails. The model uses inductive coupling across the train–track gap. The loop is a data conductor, separate from running rails, traction supply and return conductors, and the LIM reaction rail.

Historical communication example; it is not the definition of all modern CBTC.

For teaching, the useful change is the hosting boundary: logical control responsibilities can be shown separately from the cabinet or computing platform containing them. A product publication is not a complete architecture specification or deployment inventory.

The loop cable, LIM reaction rail and DC supply conductors serve different purposes. A train with rotary traction can use loop communication too. Roof radio equipment may still serve operational voice or passenger services when control uses the loop.

Fire and life safety systems (FLSS)

FLSS describes coordinated protective functions across the station and trainway.

Fire and life safety systems (FLSS) encompass several functions: recognizing a hazardous condition, notifying people, supporting escape and managing fire-related effects. Rail guidance addresses stations and trainways together with ventilation, communications and control systems.

These functions are distributed across equipment and physical spaces. A fire panel, a pump, an illuminated exit route and a ventilation plant are not interchangeable parts of one box. Their interfaces and design objectives must be understood together.

This educational grouping is not a code-compliant station design or a declaration of control authority.

National Fire Protection Association

Inspect the equipment →
Fire detection and alarm control panel

The panel organizes initiating-device information and configured outputs.

A fire control panel contains processing, interface and power-supply functions. It receives initiating-device information and distinguishes alarm, supervisory and trouble events.

Output interfaces can connect notification and other configured functions. A station supervisory screen may display panel information, but the display is not the detector loop or the fire panel itself.

Siemens

Inspect the equipment →
Fire initiating devices

Smoke, heat, manual and waterflow inputs report different kinds of evidence.

Detection devices and other initiating inputs supply information to a fire alarm system. A reported smoke or heat condition, a manual input and a waterflow indication describe different events.

An address or zone helps locate the report. The device is a measurement or initiating point; it does not by itself constitute the full station response. Its message should be visually distinct from an equipment command.

Siemens

Inspect the equipment →
Audible, visual and voice notification

Notification translates a system event into information people can perceive.

Notification may use audible devices, visual appliances or voice messages. A control interface links the event logic to the selected notification outputs; a speaker and a strobe perform different communication tasks.

Voice-alarm equipment can supervise audio paths and power availability. Sharing speakers with routine announcements is an implementation choice that needs an engineered priority arrangement; ordinary PA capability alone does not establish an emergency communication design.

Siemens · Bosch / Keenfinity Group

Inspect the equipment →
Sprinkler piping and heat-responsive heads

A conventional sprinkler head responds locally to heat.

A closed, heat-responsive sprinkler contains a thermal element that releases when its designed thermal conditions are reached. Heat response and water-distribution characteristics are part of selecting the sprinkler for its application.

This is different from a smoke detector sending an electronic alarm message. The illustrated piping supplies water to individual heads; it should not show every head opening simply because a detector reports smoke. Other suppression arrangements exist and are outside this simplified example.

National Fire Protection Association

Inspect the equipment →
Fire-water supply and pump equipment

A pump supplies pressure and flow to an engineered fire-water network.

Fire pumps move water through piping to the suppression system. A pump assembly includes the hydraulic machine, a driver and a dedicated control arrangement; water availability and electrical or other driving energy are separate dependencies.

Pressure-related signals can form part of automatic pump control. The pump controller has a different job from a general station dashboard: monitoring a pump status does not make that dashboard the complete pump-control system.

No water-storage volume, pressure setpoint, pump sequence or operating instruction is specified.

Grundfos

Inspect the equipment →
Emergency lighting and illuminated wayfinding

Lighting can retain a designated supply when normal lighting power is unavailable.

A self-contained emergency luminaire has its own battery and charging arrangement. A central-battery system supplies remote luminaires from a separate battery installation. Both are real architectures, so the model should identify which example is being shown.

The illuminated fitting is only the visible endpoint of its supply and monitoring arrangement. Its purpose and circuit classification differ from ordinary decorative lighting; a generic electronics UPS should not automatically be portrayed as the approved source for every emergency luminaire.

Eaton

Inspect the equipment →
Passenger help points and emergency communications

A help point creates a two-way conversation with an appropriate operator.

A passenger help point connects someone at a known location with an assigned answering service. Its button, microphone, loudspeaker and call electronics have different functions.

In Calls and radio, open the front panel to inspect the audio board and transducers. The illustrative call cycle distinguishes a pressed button, a pending request and an established two-way conversation.

Recipients, priorities and response arrangements depend on the railway. The model makes no call, promises no answer time and teaches no emergency procedure.

Zenitel · Zenitel

Inspect the equipment →
Passenger circulation and egress context

Levels, routes and information belong in the station systems picture.

Passenger circulation connects platform, concourse, stairs, lift landings, information and assistance. The broader station environment also contains equipment rooms and service access.

The model leaves clear boarding strips, lands its stairs at the concourse and cuts a shaft opening around the lift. These spatial relationships support explanation; they do not establish evacuation capacity, accessibility compliance or an approved route.

Do not present the model as evacuation guidance for any real station.

National Fire Protection Association

Inspect the equipment →
Tunnel ventilation fan

A fan adds mechanical energy to air and helps establish a designed airflow.

Rail tunnels receive heat from trains and electrical equipment. Powered ventilation can supplement natural effects and train-induced air movement; large axial fans and other arrangements are used according to the tunnel design.

A rotating impeller produces a pressure rise, while the connected tunnel, shaft and fittings resist the flow. Motor rotation alone is therefore not a measured airflow. In an explanatory model, the air arrows represent an intended path rather than a calculated fan duty.

FläktGroup

Inspect the equipment →
Ventilation shafts and air paths

A shaft connects the tunnel ventilation arrangement to another air volume or outdoors.

A ventilation shaft and its connected ductwork provide a physical route for supply or exhaust air. Fan rooms, dampers and openings become part of that route; the arrangement depends on station and tunnel geometry.

A moving train can also displace air. The shaft should therefore be understood as part of a pressure-connected environment, not as a guaranteed one-way chimney. The illustrated route is one selected mechanical arrangement, not a universal station cross-section.

FläktGroup · ASHRAE

Inspect the equipment →
Tunnel ventilation and smoke-control damper

Movable blades change the available air path.

A tunnel damper uses a frame and moving blades to open, restrict or isolate an air passage. Dampers intended for smoke-control duties have application-specific performance requirements; an ordinary comfort-air damper is not automatically equivalent.

The mechanical blade position, its actuator command and any reported position are separate ideas. A model can show these together without implying that a commanded position proves airflow or that every damper must take the same position during a fire.

TROX Group

Inspect the equipment →
Smoke-management objectives

Emergency ventilation is designed around conditions and routes, not simply maximum fan speed.

Normal ventilation addresses everyday heat and air-quality conditions. Emergency smoke management has different objectives, including conditions that support escape and emergency response. Fire location, geometry and the connected air paths affect what a useful ventilation strategy looks like.

Colored air or smoke traces explain objectives. They cannot establish tenability, smoke-layer height, exposure or evacuation performance, and should not prescribe a universal fan direction.

This model performs no CFD, fire-growth calculation or life-safety performance assessment.

ASHRAE

Inspect the equipment →
Station HVAC and environmental zones

Passenger spaces and equipment rooms can have different environmental needs.

Station heating, ventilation and air conditioning manages occupied spaces and the environments required by equipment. A station can combine conditioned rooms with platform areas influenced by tunnel airflow; one room thermostat does not describe the whole station.

The useful teaching distinction is the service boundary: a local air-handling system treats and distributes air for its zones, while tunnel ventilation addresses a different connected space. Some equipment can have more than one duty, but its approved operating strategy remains project-specific.

ASHRAE · Trane

Inspect the equipment →
Air-handling unit cutaway

Filters, coils, dampers and a fan perform different parts of air treatment.

An air-handling unit moves air through treatment components and into distribution ductwork. Filters remove particles; coils exchange heat with another medium; dampers regulate air paths; the fan supplies the energy needed to move the air.

Heating or cooling energy is supplied through the wider plant, such as a water or refrigerant circuit. The fan does not create cooling by itself. Component order, outside-air mixing and return-air arrangements vary, so the cutaway is one functional example.

Trane

Inspect the equipment →
Building automation controller

A controller connects field measurements to configured equipment actions and status.

A building automation system (BAS), also called a building management system (BMS) in many contexts, can include distributed controllers, input/output interfaces and supervisory software. Controllers can support schedules, alarms, trends and connections to HVAC or other building-service equipment.

Local control logic and the supervisory presentation occupy different roles. A screen can show a temperature and request a change, while the controller and its equipment interfaces implement the configured behavior. The model should show both levels rather than making a workstation the direct actuator.

Siemens · ABB

Inspect the equipment →
Building-services sensors

Sensors turn physical conditions into information for monitoring and control.

Room, duct and pipe sensors can measure different quantities, including temperature, humidity, pressure, air quality and flow. Their physical placement determines what part of the building system a reading describes.

A duct-pressure reading is not a room-temperature reading, and neither is a fire alarm by definition. In the model, selecting a sensor should highlight its measured medium and the controller input that receives its signal, rather than suggesting that all sensor symbols are interchangeable.

Belimo

Inspect the equipment →
Building-services actuators

An actuator turns a control request into a physical change.

Building control can adjust dampers, valves and fan operation to change air treatment and distribution. The physical actuator is the link between a control signal and equipment movement or modulation.

A command to move and feedback about the achieved condition are different signals. The model can expose a damper linkage or valve stem to make that distinction visible. Comfort-control equipment should not acquire a fire/smoke-control role simply because the graphics use a similar symbol.

Trane · Siemens

Inspect the equipment →
Building automation network

Field and supervisory communications connect different levels of building control.

Automation controllers can exchange data through several interface families. BACnet and Modbus are examples supported by commercial controllers; a plant can also include direct I/O connections to sensors and actuators.

The protocol name describes a communications arrangement, not a physical cable route or a universal safety classification. A useful diagram distinguishes local field connections from the station-wide supervisory link and labels both as information paths.

Siemens

Inspect the equipment →
Traction power SCADA

Supervisory control and data acquisition provides a system-level view of traction power equipment.

Power SCADA collects and presents traction-supply states, measurements and alarms, and supports authorized supervisory control functions. Its field interfaces connect the network-level view with substation equipment and local control systems.

Local protection and equipment control remain distinct engineering functions even when one vendor integrates them. A breaker symbol on an operator screen represents equipment information and an interface; it is not the interrupting device, the measurement sensor or the complete protection chain.

Do not infer a universal RTU/IED partition, trip path or remote/local command priority.

Siemens Mobility

Inspect the equipment →
Station and communications supervisory systems

A supervisory application brings selected facility and communications states into an operator view.

Station supervision presents information from local controllers and other integrated station systems. A field measurement, supervisory request, returned indication and historical record are distinct objects.

Open SCADA interfaces to follow a local position contact into an input module, RTU, gateway and HMI. Compare a command with its feedback and a stale last-known display with the current field position.

Local control, protection and other safety functions remain outside this simplified supervisory example. The topology locates logical roles without prescribing their deployment.

Naming and system boundaries vary by project; station SCADA is not a universal replacement for fire controls or BAS logic.

Transport for NSW · Siemens · Siemens Mobility · Siemens Mobility

Inspect the equipment →
Operations control centre supervisory workstation

An operator interface presents selected systems, events and communications.

A control-centre workstation provides a human interface to supervisory applications and communications. Different views can present equipment state, events, history or conversations, while servers and field equipment perform other parts of the system.

Combining information helps an operator relate events across subsystems. It does not make every indication equally current or give every user the same authority. The teaching view should distinguish observed state, unavailable data and a request whose completion has not yet been confirmed.

Siemens Mobility · Zenitel

Inspect the equipment →
Station auxiliary transformer

A building-supply transformer serves auxiliary distribution in this selected example.

A medium-to-low-voltage transformer can supply the building-services distribution system. Its input supply, magnetic conversion and output distribution are distinct parts of the power path.

This example separates auxiliary supply from the traction rectifier branch. That helps explain why station lighting and electronics need their own distribution arrangements. Real projects can use different supply topologies, transformer locations and redundancy schemes.

Schneider Electric, Electrical Installation Guide

Inspect the equipment →
Auxiliary electrical distribution

Busbars and protective outgoing circuits distribute power to station loads.

A low-voltage main switchboard receives the transformer output and distributes electrical supply through protected circuits. Main and branch equipment serve different parts of the installation.

Essential loads may be organized separately, and an alternative supply or UPS can be included where the design requires it. In the model, selected electronics, lighting and mechanical plant should have visibly distinct branches rather than all appearing to run through one small backup battery.

Schneider Electric, Electrical Installation Guide

Inspect the equipment →
Uninterruptible power supply for selected electronics

Backup power can keep designated control and communications electronics available.

A station UPS can support sensitive electronics such as controllers, I/O equipment and user interfaces when the normal supply is disturbed. Its protected load boundary is part of the design.

Keeping a supervisory screen alive does not prove that every associated motor, fan or field device still has power. The teaching model should trace the selected backed-up circuits separately from the larger auxiliary loads and avoid implying unlimited battery endurance.

ABB

Inspect the equipment →
Station telecommunications rack

The rack houses network and service equipment; it is not itself a protocol.

A rack provides a physical mounting context for equipment whose functions remain distinct: fibre termination, switching, routing, application interfaces and power.

The station alternative contains separate passive and powered assemblies with removable trays, boards, modules and supply components. Enclosures can be opened without treating the whole rack as one opaque box.

Rack count, ventilation, resilience and service allocation are original teaching choices, not an operator installation.

Moxa · Westermo · ABB

Inspect the equipment →
Fiber-optic backhaul and backbone

Fiber carries information between network nodes and distant system locations.

Fiber links connect communications equipment over the wider rail network. Backhaul links can carry station or radio-node traffic toward shared services and control-centre applications.

A fiber route is a physical path. The services using it are logical traffic relationships; drawing several services together does not specify their segregation or resilience.

Moxa

Inspect the equipment →
Station network switch

An active network device connects local endpoints and upstream links.

The local switch connects equipment ports to an Ethernet network. Copper ports, optical transceivers, the circuit board and power input are distinct physical parts.

Open Network equipment to separate the switch lid, board and transceiver. Follow the patch lead to the passive fibre panel and the wider network boundary.

The illustrative ports do not define capacity, addressing, traffic separation or a cyber-security policy.

Westermo · Moxa

Inspect the equipment →
Platform trainway intrusion detection

Monitors a defined track area for a person or object that should not be there.

At an open platform, intrusion detection observes the trainway rather than physically closing the platform edge. The evaluated FTA example sends warnings to railway systems and personnel when its monitored track area is intruded upon.

A visible object, a detection decision and an operational response are different steps. The model shows their interfaces without asserting that every intrusion causes the same automatic brake command.

Detection is not a barrier or a guarantee that an approaching train can stop; coverage and response are project-specific.

Federal Transit Administration / Transportation Technology Center / Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority

Inspect the equipment →
Platform LiDAR sensor and monitored volume

Laser ranging samples the space around the track as a three-dimensional point cloud.

Platform-mounted LiDAR measures distance to form a three-dimensional point cloud. Siemens describes overlapping sensors for observing track danger zones.

The rendered volume illustrates coverage; it is not a validated sensor envelope.

No field of view, minimum detectable object, detection probability or environmental performance is specified.

Siemens Mobility

Inspect the equipment →
Paired radar intrusion-detection plane

A transmitter and receiver arrangement detects an interruption across the track area.

FTA Report 0189 describes transmitter/receiver pairs on opposite sides of the track. An intruding object interrupts their radar path at a plane beneath the platform edge and above the rail.

The evaluated system also processes detections to distinguish unwanted activations, including a train passing through the area. This differs from recognizing every object with an ordinary passenger CCTV camera.

The rendered beams are schematic; heights, spacing, thresholds and filtering logic are not installation instructions.

Federal Transit Administration / Transportation Technology Center / Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority

Inspect the equipment →
Associated platform camera and video

An associated camera supplies a separate view of the reported location.

Siemens describes an operator seeing live and historical video associated with an intrusion alarm location.

The selectable hardware here is the platform camera, mounted at the rear of the passenger area. Its event marker identifies an associated video relationship; the operator workstation belongs in the control-centre study. The camera image is not used as proof of track clearance.

The site does not provide incident-response instructions or retention rules.

Siemens Mobility

Inspect the equipment →
Detection processor and train-control interface

A local processor reports sensor evidence through a defined railway interface.

The Siemens example separates perception processing, railway interfaces and associated video. The selected LiDAR and paired-radar examples are alternatives; the scene does not imply both are always installed.

The local processor sits in a rear service alcove. The phase sequence changes sensor evidence before the report marker. The object remains in place after reporting; acknowledging or viewing a report cannot remove it.

The model illustrates ordering with invented delays. It does not implement object classification, health logic, a railway protocol or a prescribed response.

Federal Transit Administration / Transportation Technology Center / Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority · Siemens Mobility

Inspect the equipment →
Platform screen or edge doors

Half-height and full-height facades provide different physical boarding boundaries.

ST Engineering publishes half-height, semi-full-height and full-height forms. The atlas compares an open edge with two original barrier geometries; selecting a sensing or end-access lesson preserves that physical choice.

The openings line up with the parked teaching vehicle. The full-height example has a header drive; the half-height example uses side-post drives. These invented mechanisms do not reproduce a supplier design or prescribe a ventilation arrangement.

The model provides no stopping tolerance, ventilation calculation, structural design or compliance claim.

ST Engineering · National Capital Region Transport Corporation

Inspect the equipment →
Door actuator and local door controller

A drive converts a request into leaf movement; feedback comes from separate equipment.

Nippon Signal describes individual door controllers that act on commands and return status. Portalp distinguishes drive control from closed and locking information.

The full-height teaching mechanism turns pulleys as the paired leaves travel. The half-height mechanism moves racks through side-post pinions, leaving the boarding opening clear. Open or separate the covers, transmission and controller to inspect their roles.

The chosen transmissions and phase timing are authored illustrations, not supplier geometry or an operating sequence.

Nippon Signal · Portalp Railway

Inspect the equipment →
Closed and locked indications

The closed contact, lock mechanism and returned indication describe different conditions.

A command, a closed leaf and locking information are separate interfaces in the Portalp example.

Pause after closing: the leaf target has returned to its contact while the bolt remains withdrawn. The bolt then engages, followed by the separate locking indication. The demonstration never derives train departure permission.

The contacts and lock are explanatory geometry, not a safety circuit, failure analysis or universal departure rule.

Portalp Railway

Inspect the equipment →
Train–platform-door interspace detection

The monitored interspace lies between the train body and a fitted platform facade.

Wabtec describes residual risk in the space between a train and platform-door facade. Nippon Signal gives an example of an optional ranging sensor on the train side of the barrier.

The model marks that volume separately from the trainway and fits the object within it. This lesson requires a barrier; an open edge has no train–facade interspace. A report does not make the object disappear.

This is neither closing-edge obstacle sensing nor a validated coverage envelope.

Nippon Signal · Wabtec

Inspect the equipment →
Platform end gate and restricted-zone monitoring

End access is a separate boundary that can accompany any selected platform edge.

Portalp describes end doors with their own control units. Restricted end and tunnel zones are separate monitoring applications in the Molinari examples.

The end-gate leaf turns around its hinge. The latch releases while the gate is still closed; opening then separates the contact target and the frame contact. The end-access report follows. Selecting this lesson preserves the open, half-height or full-height boarding edge.

The phase sequence explains hardware relationships. It supplies no access permission, emergency-release or track-entry procedure.

Portalp Railway · Molinari Sensors

Inspect the equipment →
Street-to-station entrance

The passenger journey begins before the platform.

An accessible station journey connects public areas and their interfaces. Step-free access is one need among several.

The fictional station links its street entrance to a wide fare gate, lift, platform and boarding point. A tactile strip and information equipment remain visible alongside the step-free path.

European Union Agency for Railways · RNIB

Inspect the equipment →
Fare-gate passage

Ticketing and physical passage meet at the gate.

Ticketing, information and the physical station environment can each create a barrier to the journey.

The wide passage is a distinct assembly with reader, gate leaves and a clear route through it. Its schematic width does not demonstrate accessibility compliance or replace a passenger’s need for assistance.

RNIB · European Union Agency for Railways

Inspect the equipment →
Lift and alternative route

An unavailable lift changes which route is usable.

Operators provide information about elevator availability because a passenger may depend on that connection.

Lift unavailable breaks the near lift route and reveals the service message while retaining the stairs. Alternate lift highlights a different step-free path through the fictional station; it does not route a wheelchair user onto the stairs.

TransLink · European Union Agency for Railways

Inspect the equipment →
Wayfinding and journey information

Physical access and understandable information work together.

Route identification, readable information and consistent assistance matter through the journey. Research with blind and partially sighted passengers identifies barriers beyond changes of level.

Tactile surfaces, an audible-information point and display are separately selectable equipment. An outage changes the route message and assistance link; those information paths do not become physical passenger routes.

European Union Agency for Railways · RNIB

Inspect the equipment →
Passenger assistance interface

A help point connects a passenger need with a person or service.

Operator guidance connects station assistance with information about the facilities available for a journey.

The help point has a distinct communications path to an assistance position. Choosing lift outage exposes that path without pretending that a displayed message or button press guarantees assistance has arrived.

TransLink · RNIB

Inspect the equipment →
Platform-to-vehicle boarding

Reaching the platform does not finish the boarding interface.

The platform edge, vehicle doorway and any boarding aid form another interface in the journey.

Compare the available route with boarding aid required. The latter retains a visible gap and stops the route at the platform. Aid in place adds a bridging plate and extends the path into the doorway. No slope, gap tolerance, capacity or evacuation result is calculated.

European Union Agency for Railways

Inspect the equipment →
Station passenger lift

The cabin connects two landings through a dedicated shaft.

The car travels within the shaft while separate landing doors remain at each floor. A clear opening in the concourse accommodates the moving assembly.

The example starts at platform level. The phase control closes the doors, moves the cabin and then opens at the upper landing. Dimensions and timing are illustrative.

KONE

Inspect the equipment →
Lift cabin and car doors

The cabin, its floor and its own doors move together.

The car is the moving passenger enclosure. Its doors travel with it; the landing doors belong to the building.

Follow the cabin floor against the two landing sills. This example opens the car doors only when its floor is aligned with a landing. No levelling tolerance or access compliance is claimed.

KONE

Inspect the equipment →
Lift landing doors and contacts

A fixed door assembly bounds the shaft at each landing.

Landing doors are distinct from the doors on the car. Their position and locking interfaces belong to the lift system.

In the model only the doors beside the aligned cabin open. Both landings stay closed during travel. The enlarged contact targets explain relative position, not a complete interlock circuit.

KONE

Inspect the equipment →
Lift traction machine and suspension

A selected traction arrangement moves the cabin and counterweight.

A traction sheave and suspension connect the drive with the moving masses. Other lift arrangements exist.

The sheave turns with cabin travel and the counterweight moves in the opposite direction. Inspect the separate machine and sheave; the original geometry supplies no suspension, braking or load calculation.

KONE

Inspect the equipment →

Control centre

Operations control centre

A physical workplace presents information from systems distributed across the railway.

Begin with the room, its consoles, shared display, cable routes and adjacent technical equipment. The same furniture remains in place when different information is presented.

Select a console or cabinet to inspect its physical parts. Information behaviour follows a request and a separately returned observation through labelled system boundaries.

People, responsibilities, incident coordination and duty handover have their own People & processes pages. No staffing quantities or operator facility layout are reproduced.

Original public-source teaching model. Layout, quantities and deployment are illustrative; the sequence is not an operating instruction.

Control-room console

The console physically supports displays, input devices, communications and their connections.

The desk is a workplace assembly. Its monitors, computer interface, keyboard, pointing device and communications terminal serve different functions.

The close view separates monitor panels, controller boards, enclosure, keyboard and interface board. The room view uses the same console without assigning a job role to its furniture.

Local computer and Remote computer compare two illustrated presentation arrangements. Moving the compute equipment does not transfer an operating responsibility.

Original public-source teaching model. Layout, quantities and deployment are illustrative; the sequence is not an operating instruction.

Local client computer

A local computer renders the application view used at the console.

In the local arrangement, the computer sits near its display and input devices. The screen is an output; the computer, application and information source are separate dependencies.

Remove the cover to see the original interface-board schematic and connector face. During the example, receipt and rendering precede the changed display pattern.

This is generic computing anatomy, not a particular workstation specification or prescribed railway architecture.

Original public-source teaching model. Layout, quantities and deployment are illustrative; the sequence is not an operating instruction.

Remote computer interface

Keyboard, video and pointing-device connections can link a workplace to computing equipment elsewhere.

Public KVM products place computers in a technical room while the display and input devices remain at a remote workplace. Other thin-client arrangements use different protocols and deployment choices.

Remote computer replaces the local computer with an interface module. Open its cover to inspect the connector board; follow the logical source and recipient in Connections.

The drawing is one possible arrangement. It does not specify access control, latency, network isolation or exclusive control.

Display distribution controller

A presentation controller connects selected information sources with display surfaces.

Control-room visualization products can supply both a workstation and a shared video wall. The presentation system distributes views; it is not the field controller being viewed.

The controller is drawn as a small hardware interface beneath the wall and in the technical cabinet. A received update appears locally before the shared-display stage.

Source selection and display availability are separate from the validity of the underlying railway information.

Original public-source teaching model. Layout, quantities and deployment are illustrative; the sequence is not an operating instruction.

Data and power cable routes

Physical connections carry data and power between the workplace and technical equipment.

Consoles and cabinets need connections as well as floor space. Cable trays organize those physical routes; their position is part of the room anatomy.

The model shows a tray, separate cable runs and connections behind equipment. It does not turn a tray into an abstract message-flow chart.

Data routes and electrical supply are different dependencies. The geometry does not specify segregation distances, fire performance or an installed cable design.

Control-room guidance connects input arrangements with readable feedback and the work being supported.

The keyboard and pointing device are independently removable parts. Their connection to the client is separate from the monitor and communications handset.

Lighting, sightlines and the surrounding room affect how a display is used.

The close view contains an empty chair, a light support and acoustic-panel proxies around the console. They supply physical context without modelling staff roles.

Host hardware runs software that receives and organizes supervisory information.

Original schematic. Equipment provision and operating arrangements depend on the fleet and facility.

Office of Rail and Road

Explore the process →
Depot personnel protection and movement inhibition

Protected work areas constrain when a vehicle movement may enter.

A published protection arrangement links personnel registration, local panels, movement indications and protective devices. Equipment can have additional interlocks.

The illustration distinguishes the physical work boundary from displayed information. It does not calculate or grant access permission.

The arrangement is an original schematic teaching model; actual equipment, staffing and procedures are site-specific.

Sentric Safety Group / Zonegreen

Inspect the equipment →
Energy isolation and access interlocking

Removing movement permission and controlling hazardous energy are separate protections.

Depot interlocking can link access gates and equipment with an electrical-isolation condition. The engineered arrangement must also address the relevant hazards of the actual vehicle and facility.

The model distinguishes three ideas: a stop indication, the physical supply state and permission to access a work area. A green screen symbol alone is not proof of absence of hazardous energy.

The arrangement is an original schematic teaching model; actual equipment, staffing and procedures are site-specific.

Zonegreen

Inspect the equipment →
Changed equipment item

Installed equipment has a configuration identity.

An assurance package connects the physical element with its design, test and as-built records.

The fictional installed version B has two connectors. The earlier A configuration is identified by a single mark on its baseline and test records. Installation alone does not update the separate baseline and test record.

Crossrail Learning Legacy

Explore the process →
Configuration baseline

The record must identify the version actually installed.

Design, as-built and test information need an identifiable subject if they are to support a changed asset.

Installed, unmatched leaves version A on the baseline while the physical module is B. Baseline matched changes the record to B but retains the old test subject. Matching records and successful testing remain separate comparisons.

Crossrail Learning Legacy

Explore the process →
Requirement and verification question

Evidence needs a question that it can answer.

Change assessment considers the defined system and the safety implications of the change within its applicable context.

The fictional requirement asks whether the replacement reports both input channels. It connects to a test record rather than directly to the acceptance record. No safety classification or formal requirement approval is performed.

Office of Rail and Road · Crossrail Learning Legacy

Explore the process →
Changed interface definition

A changed connector can affect more than the replaceable module.

A change can affect interfaces and supporting records as well as the component being replaced.

The second connector and cable appear with version B. The interface sheet shows two connection points, while the old test record still refers to the earlier one-channel subject until the test comparison changes.

Crossrail Learning Legacy · Office of Rail and Road

Explore the process →
Test subject and result

A passing result for version A is not a result for version B.

The public record-package example includes test information alongside design, construction and as-built records.

Test recorded replaces the old subject card and connects two channel traces to the version B record. An open issue remains. The illustrated pass marker concerns this fictional check alone, not all reliability, availability, maintainability or safety evidence.

Crossrail Learning Legacy

Explore the process →
Outstanding issues and RAMS questions

Different assurance questions can remain open after a functional check.

Evidence for a change can include unresolved issues and limits that must be considered by the responsible parties.

The issue board separates reliability, availability, maintainability and safety questions. A maintainability-access issue remains in the tested comparison. Reviewed handover adds an explicit disposition record rather than erasing that history.

Crossrail Learning Legacy · Office of Rail and Road

Explore the process →
Reviewed handover record

Evidence review and acceptance are accountable decisions.

Regulatory change assessment and project handover have defined responsibilities. Their exact process depends on the jurisdiction and project.

Reviewed handover adds a fictional decision record connected to the B baseline, B test and issue disposition. It does not approve a real change, decide regulatory significance or grant movement permission.
